title: Do 97% of Day Traders Really Lose Money?

scenes.purpose: Open on the promise in the trader's own words.

visual.description: Quote card: the quoted words only, 'disciplined, consistent strategy' held in accent colour as it is spoken.
onScreenText: "showing you what's possible if you follow a disciplined, consistent strategy"

scenes.direction: Cold open; words type on with the narration.
scenes.narration: On YouTube, Riley Coleman films himself growing a tiny futures account, and says the point is "showing you what's possible if you follow a disciplined, consistent strategy".

scenes.purpose: Pose the question the video answers.

visual.description: The question types on in large type; 'end up ahead' held a beat in accent colour.
onScreenText: How many of the people who try actually end up ahead?

scenes.direction: Type on with the narration; hold 0.5 s.
scenes.narration: If discipline is what it takes, how many of the people who try actually end up ahead?

scenes.purpose: Name the two studies that counted everyone, winners included.

visual.description: A single title line: 'Brazil and Taiwan', 'counted' punching in under it.
onScreenText: Researchers in Brazil and Taiwan counted

scenes.direction: Camera punch on 'counted'.
scenes.narration: Researchers in Brazil and Taiwan counted, and they counted the winners too.

scenes.purpose: The pitch from a trading educator: borrow a proven strategy.

visual.description: Quote card: quoted words only; 'no guarantee it'll work for you' dims slightly as it is spoken.
onScreenText: "learn a strategy that is proven profitable by someone else even if there's no guarantee it'll work for you"

scenes.direction: Hard cut in from the title.
scenes.narration: Ross Cameron of Warrior Trading tells beginners to "learn a strategy that is proven profitable by someone else even if there's no guarantee it'll work for you".

scenes.purpose: The bluntest version of the pitch.

visual.description: Quote card: quoted words only, 'The math is real' held in accent colour.
onScreenText: "The strategy is real. The math is real, and there's people using it right now to make money."

scenes.direction: Camera push on 'make money'.
scenes.narration: Another channel, RP Profits, is blunter: "The strategy is real. The math is real, and there's people using it right now to make money."

scenes.purpose: The same educator's blog concedes most lose: the tension.

visual.description: Quote card: quoted words only; 'most day traders lose money' turns amber as it is spoken.
onScreenText: "Trading is risky, and most day traders lose money."

scenes.direction: Hold 1 s after the last word.
scenes.narration: Yet the Warrior Trading blog itself carries the line "Trading is risky, and most day traders lose money."

scenes.purpose: Set up who the Brazilian study followed.

visual.description: The study's abstract, the line about who it observed highlighted.

excerpt.highlight: who began to day trade between 2013 and 2015 in the Brazilian equity futures market

citations.label: Chague et al., Brazil day-trader study

scenes.direction: Highlight sweeps on 'began day trading'.
scenes.narration: The Brazilian study followed people who began day trading in the country's equity futures market between 2013 and 2015, and sorted them by how many days they kept at it.

scenes.purpose: Show the share in profit falling with every step of persistence.

visual.description: Horizontal bars, one per group by days traded, top to bottom from one day to more than 300; the first bar lands on '29.8 percent', the rest shrink in sequence on 'fell at every step'.

chart.title: Share who made a net profit, by days traded
chart.note: Each bar is a different group of people (by how long they traded), not the same people over time.

citations.label: Chague et al., new day traders in Brazil by days traded

scenes.direction: Bars build top to bottom; the group labels are read off the chart, give them a beat to settle.
scenes.narration: Of those who tried it for a single day, 29.8 percent made a net profit, and the share fell at every step after that.

scenes.purpose: The authors' own comparison: roulette.

visual.description: The study passage with the roulette comparison highlighted.

excerpt.highlight: the proportion of successful players also monotonically decreases with the number of rounds played

citations.label: Chague et al., Brazil day-trader study

scenes.direction: Highlight on 'roulette'.
scenes.narration: The authors compare it to roulette, where the more rounds people play, the fewer come out ahead.

scenes.purpose: The persistent traders: almost all lost.

visual.description: Three tiles build one by one as spoken: 1,551 who kept going, 97% lost after fees, 47 came out ahead.

chart.title: Traded more than 300 days
chart.note: Net of exchange and brokerage fees.

citations.label: Chague et al., 1,551 persistent day traders

scenes.direction: Camera punch on '97 percent'; hold 1 s after the last tile.
scenes.narration: Of the 1,551 who kept going for more than 300 days, 97 percent lost money after fees, and only 47 came out ahead.

scenes.purpose: Even the winners earned little.

visual.description: Two tiles: 17 above minimum wage, then $310 a day for the single best.

chart.title: The winners
chart.note: Out of the 1,551 persistent day traders.

citations.label: Chague et al., earnings of persistent traders

scenes.direction: Tiles land on '17' and '310 dollars'.
scenes.narration: Only 17 earned more than Brazil's minimum wage, and the single best averaged 310 dollars a day.

scenes.purpose: The few above a bank teller's pay rode large daily swings.

visual.description: Two tiles for the range of daily swings among the eight who beat a bank teller's pay: lowest and highest standard deviation.

chart.title: Daily swings of those above a bank teller's pay
chart.note: Standard deviation of daily profit, per trader.

citations.label: Chague et al., volatility of the top earners

scenes.direction: Camera shakes lightly on 'roller coaster'.
scenes.narration: And the handful who beat a bank teller's starting pay got there on a roller coaster, their daily results swinging by hundreds to thousands of dollars.

scenes.purpose: Ask whether practice helped.

visual.description: The question types on.
onScreenText: Did the ones who stayed get better with practice?

scenes.direction: Type on; hold 0.5 s.
scenes.narration: Did the ones who stayed at least get better with practice?

scenes.purpose: The answer: no evidence of learning.

visual.description: The abstract with the no-learning finding highlighted.

excerpt.highlight: no evidence of learning by day trading

citations.label: Chague et al., Brazil day-trader study

scenes.direction: Highlight on 'no evidence'; hold 1 s.
scenes.narration: The study found no evidence that they learned.

scenes.purpose: Bring in the second study, Taiwan.

visual.description: The Taiwan study abstract, 'the vast majority of day traders are unprofitable' highlighted.

excerpt.highlight: the vast majority of day traders are unprofitable

citations.label: Barber et al., Taiwan day traders 1992 to 2006

scenes.direction: Wipe from the Brazil excerpt; highlight on 'vast majority'.
scenes.narration: A second study, of individual investors who day traded in Taiwan from 1992 to 2006, found the vast majority of them unprofitable.

scenes.purpose: Costs more than triple the daily loss.

visual.description: Two tiles: 7 basis points a day before costs, then 23.9 after costs, the second tile visibly larger.

chart.title: Average daily loss, in basis points
chart.note: A basis point is a hundredth of a percent; day traders as a group.

citations.label: Barber et al., aggregate day-trader returns

scenes.direction: Second tile lands on '23.9' with a punch.
scenes.narration: Taken as a group, they lost 7 basis points a day before costs, where a basis point is a hundredth of a percent, and trading costs more than tripled that loss, to 23.9.

scenes.purpose: Turn: is anyone reliably good?

visual.description: The question types on.
onScreenText: So is anyone reliably good at this?

scenes.direction: Type on; hold 0.5 s.
scenes.narration: So is anyone reliably good at this?

scenes.purpose: Yes: a few past winners kept winning.

visual.description: The Taiwan passage, the finding on experienced profitable traders highlighted.

excerpt.highlight: earn more than enough to cover their transaction costs

citations.label: Barber et al., persistence of profitability

scenes.direction: Highlight on 'earn more than their trading costs'.
scenes.narration: A few are: in Taiwan, traders who had already been profitable, with more than 40 days of day trading in the past year, went on to earn more than their trading costs.

scenes.purpose: But they were a sliver of everyone.

visual.description: A 10 by 10 waffle; fewer than 3 squares light up in accent colour, the rest stay grey.

chart.title: Predictably profitable, share of day traders on an average day
chart.note: An upper bound: the study says less than 3%.

citations.label: Barber et al., predictably profitable traders

scenes.direction: Squares light on 'less than 3 percent'; hold 1 s.
scenes.narration: But those predictably profitable traders made up less than 3 percent of all day traders on an average day.

scenes.purpose: An educator names one reason: the algorithms on the other side.

visual.description: Quote card: quoted words only, 'you really don't have a good edge' in accent colour.
onScreenText: "when you trade against the high frequency trading algorithms, trading large caps, you really don't have a good edge"

scenes.direction: Hard cut in.
scenes.narration: Ross Cameron names one reason the rest struggle: "when you trade against the high frequency trading algorithms, trading large caps, you really don't have a good edge".

scenes.purpose: The Brazil data agree: more high-frequency trading, bigger losses for individuals.

visual.description: Two tiles: '+10%' share of deals by high-frequency traders, then '19%' higher average loss for individuals, joined by an arrow.

chart.title: When high-frequency trading rises

points.label: rise in high-frequency traders' share of deals

chart.note: An association in the Brazilian futures data, not a controlled experiment.

citations.label: Chague et al., high-frequency traders and individual losses

scenes.direction: Second tile lands on '19 percent'; hold 1 s before the answer.
scenes.narration: The Brazilian futures data point the same way in a different market: when high-frequency traders' share of deals rose by 10 percent, individuals' average loss was 19 percent higher.

scenes.purpose: The answer in two lines.

visual.description: Two lines build one per sentence.
onScreenText: In both studies, most people lost
Some beat the odds, a sliver of everyone who tried

citations.label: Chague et al., Brazil day-trader study
Barber et al., Taiwan day-trader study

scenes.direction: Line one on 'most people lost', line two on 'a sliver'.
scenes.narration: So yes: in both studies most people lost, and in Brazil the longer they kept at it, the worse their odds of being ahead. Some people do beat the odds, and in Taiwan the ones who had been winning tended to keep winning, but they were a sliver of everyone who tried.

scenes.purpose: What the studies cannot tell you.

visual.description: Two lines build one per sentence, in a quieter colour.
onScreenText: Neither confirmed nor ruled out: one trader's month

scenes.direction: Line one on 'other markets', line two on 'neither confirmed nor ruled out'.
scenes.narration: Both studies looked at other markets and other years than today's American stock market, so they give the odds there, not a law for every market. What these counts can't do is check any one trader's month: a screenshot of a small account turned into a big one is neither confirmed nor ruled out by a tally of everyone who tried.

scenes.purpose: Two things to do.

visual.description: Two lines build one per sentence.
onScreenText: Ask for audited results across every account and every month
Only what you can afford to lose; judge by results after fees

scenes.direction: Line one on 'audited results', line two on 'afford to lose'; hold 1.5 s at the end.
scenes.narration: If someone sells you a strategy as consistent, ask for audited results across every account and every month, not the best screenshot. And if you try it anyway, put in only what you can afford to lose, and judge yourself by your results after fees, not by your best day.
